Routine oil at Paul's regular shop (Express Oil, Moreland Ave) on live coupons — and a FREE second-opinion look at the coolant leak while it's on the lift. GATE FIRST (call 404-659-6225): confirm they stock VW 502.00-approved oil (5W-40 preferred; a 502.00 5W-30 is also fine) + get the out-the-door price with $20-off — the coupon covers standard oil only and voids with customer-supplied oil, so gate on VW 502.00 (a 502.00 5W-30 is fine, 5W-40 preferred for the Stage-1 tune) — the real walk-away is a generic/dexos 5W-30 with NO 502.00 (then walk to Autobahn). If oil's a go: stack the FREE tire rotation (RTE026) + $15-off alignment (ASR026), and ask them to inspect + pressure-test the coolant leak (known EA888 failure = plastic water pump + thermostat housing). Coolant is VW G13 (pink) ONLY — if they don't stock it, inspect only, add nothing. Get any leak finding + repair estimate IN WRITING as a benchmark vs Autobahn. Coupons: $39.99 conv / $59.99 hi-mileage (YID726, thru 7/11) or $20-off (YDCD26, thru 7/31); free rotation + alignment thru 7/31. Full question list: .research/2026-07-08-gti-express-oil-coupons.md.

Done — running NGK R7437-8 racing plugs (the APR Stage-1 heat range), installed and doing well. These are one range colder than stock; the R7437-9 Eurofed used with the 2022 tune is the Stage-3 plug (over-cold here) and is now hard to find, so the -8 is the correct pick, not a compromise. NEXT CHANGE reminder: gap to 0.024" (they ship at 0.028" — close them down), torque ~25 Nm / 18 ft-lb dry (no anti-seize — NGK's plating already anti-seizes), dielectric grease in the coil boots, and change roughly every ~20k mi on the tune. Full spec + sources in .research/2026-07-14-gti-spark-plug-setup.md. ORIGIN (7/23 ingest): Jim Ellis quoted a $348 plug job on the 3/20/2025 estimate; Paul declined and ordered the 4x NGK R7437-8 himself five days later — declined-dealer-work-then-DIY, documented.

Get a second key before you ever need it — you still have one working key, so this is a cheap “add-a-key” job, not the all-keys-lost nightmare. Yours is the flip-key-with-KESSY (Comfort Access) type — SPEC CONFIRMED off Paul's own key (2026-07-14, read off the fob + web-verified): genuine Hella OEM, FCC ID NBGFS12P01, VW part 5G0 959 752 BE family (MK7 / MQB platform), 315 MHz US, MQB48 transponder, HU66 blade, CR2025 battery, 4-button. ⚠️ THIS CORRECTS AN EARLIER SPEC: the Facebook Marketplace pair read 5K0 837 202 AK / FCC NBG010206T — a DIFFERENT, older (non-MK7) generation. Do NOT buy those for this car; they're the wrong key and would be the classic won't-program money-pit. Source to NBGFS12P01 / 5G0 959 752. Two routes: a VW-capable MOBILE locksmith (comes to you, one visit, ~$250–400, roughly 40–60% under dealer) or a VW dealer (either Jim Ellis Chamblee — right by Autobahn, so you can do it the same trip as the GTI service — or Jim Ellis Kennesaw, which is on the way to the property; OEM but usually order-then-return = 2 trips, ~$350–450; bundle it with the free 16V647 recall check + a written 90k estimate). The catch with USED keys (e.g. a Facebook Marketplace pair): the MK7 is MQB, so registering a key needs dealer FAZIT online access or an MQB-capable locksmith, and a used fob still married to another car can REFUSE to program (people have burned $120+ trying). Before buying used, confirm it’s virgin/resettable AND line up someone who’ll program used MQB keys — otherwise a new aftermarket NBGFS12P01 / 5G0 959 752 fob (~$35–80) programs clean. Programming is the gated cost either way (~$60–150). On the dealer trip: skip any "free multi-point inspection" as a to-do list (dealer pricing + upsell, and you trust Autobahn for the real diagnosis) — but DO grab the dealer-only freebies: the free recall check + any recall work (16V647 EVAP etc.), and optionally a free written estimate to use as a price benchmark against Autobahn. While it's there for the freebies, it costs nothing to have them also eyeball the two open 'verify at next visit' items — the coolant level and the brake-pad thickness — just don't let those turn into an upsell list. — RECALL NOTE: a suction-jet-pump safety recall was already performed at Jim Ellis 3/2025 (@ ~73.6k); still worth running a fresh free recall check by VIN on the dealer trip in case anything new has been issued.

Paul does these himself (DIY) — not an Autobahn job. Engine air filter: VW OEM 5Q0 129 620 B. Cabin filter: VW OEM 5Q0 819 644 A (activated-carbon combination filter). Both are easy at-home swaps; pick them up and do them at the property.

Direct injection builds carbon on the intake valves; 80–100k is the window to inspect and walnut-blast — at ~81k you're just at the front edge, so it may well not be needed yet. Have the shop scope it and tell you how bad it is before you commit to the job.
No fixed interval; stretch usually needs action at 120–150k. A quick VCDS / OBDeleven read now gives a baseline — worth it on a tuned car.
Both are common softening/failure points on tuned MK7s. Cheap to inspect while it's at this visit.

restoration.detail: The rear swing-out carrier (the aftermarket one that doubles as a step) is disassembled and its hinge hardware is off. IDENTIFIED 2026-08-04: a pin-and-barrel hinge — a 1/2" pin down through flanged bushings seated in counterbored eyes, two hinges stacked, both halves WELDED (eye to the arm, clevis ears to the mount). INSPECTED: nothing worn — bores unworn, counterbores intact, no thread damage. So NO PARTS ARE NEEDED. What the parts actually are is DRY: there is no grease fitting anywhere in this design, so it ran unlubricated for decades, and dry reads as ruined without being ruined. The job is clean, grease, reassemble. ⭐ The pin is a PIVOT, not a clamp — snug it until the arm swings freely with no slop and retain with a nyloc; free rotation is the acceptance test, not a torque figure. Anti-seize the threads: with no zerks, a teardown is the only lubrication chance this hinge ever gets. 💰 COST/TIME ESTIMATE (researched 2026-07-27). THREE THINGS MAKE THIS A CHEAP RUST REPAIR, and they belong up front: the bed floor is NOT frame-structural (so a bonded patch is legitimate — no welding, which is the usual cost cliff); it ends up UNDER CARPET; and the truck is being resprayed anyway (no blending or colour-match problem). Finish standard = SOUND AND SEALED, not invisible.
• A — surface scale, no perforation (the lean from the photo): ONE AFTERNOON, 3–5 hrs, $40–80 materials (flap disc/wire wheel, rust converter or phosphoric etch, epoxy primer, seam sealer). DIY, no shop.
• B — localized perforation, pinholes to ~fist-sized: DIY bonded patch = A WEEKEND, 8–12 hrs across two sessions (adhesive cure). $100–180 (18–20ga sheet, 3M panel adhesive, cutoff wheels, sealer, primer). Shop-welded ≈ $300–700 metro Atlanta — forum quotes of 2–3 hrs @ $35–45/hr are DATED; small independents here run $60–120/hr.
• C — the wet spread further than it looks: repro panels EXIST and are CHEAP (Raybuck 1980–96 Ford full-size bed floor repair section; patch panels generally $40–100) — the panel is never the cost, the LABOUR is. Shop cut-and-weld $800–2,000. The ~$2,500 figure that floats around forums is comprehensive floor replacement, not a corner.

MOST LIKELY: A, possibly a small B — an afternoon to a weekend, $50–180, no shop. ⚠️ CAVEAT, and it's Paul's own rule already in guides/bolores-bodywork-rust-dents.md: A BUBBLE IS THE TIP, NOT THE EXTENT — scope AFTER grinding back to clean metal, never off the surface. And the real cost of guessing wrong here is CALENDAR, not dollars: this is Phase 1, and Phase 1 gates the whole repaint.

THREE OPTIONS (researched 2026-07-27; all prices owner-reported on forums, NOT verified from a vendor page — re-check before ordering):
A. RECOVER THE ORIGINAL BOARDS — ~$96–100 shipped for foam-backed cloth covering BOTH panels. Pull the boards, strip the old fabric, WIRE-BRUSH the dead foam completely off (the step people underestimate — leave powder and nothing sticks), 3M headliner adhesive on both surfaces, let it tack, lay the material. A few hours; work in shade so the adhesive doesn't flash. Cheapest by 3×, keeps the factory attachment points — but it does NOT fix the board. The original substrate is compressed fiberboard; if it's warped, water-stained, or brittle at the edges (plausible on a truck with a known water-intrusion history) it will sag again. A thin fiberglass coat on the back stiffens it, but adds real mess and time.
B. PRE-COVERED ABS BOARD — ~$335 shipped (LMR) to ~$450 + ~$50 shipping. Vacuum-formed at 320°F so it won't distort in Georgia heat, covered in ¼" foam-backed cloth, uses factory attachment points, and PERMANENTLY ends the sagging problem — ABS doesn't absorb water. Sold by LMR, LMC, Headliner Express, Stock Interiors, Bronco Graveyard, OC Auto Carpets, JEGS, Auto Obsession. Risk is SHIPPING: big rigid panels, often freight/oversize, and damaged-in-transit is the recurring complaint — inspect at delivery.
C. UNCOVERED ABS + COVER IT YOURSELF — new permanent substrate, you pick the fabric. The fallback if no stock color matches the leather.

LEANING B (ABS). Same converge-the-teardown logic that made the paint call: a full interior refinish is already underway on a truck with a documented water problem, so ~$350 once to make the headliner a solved-forever problem fits. BUT the deciding fact only exists with the boards down — if they come out flat and solid, A is legitimate. Judge it during teardown.

LAYER MODEL (researched 2026-07-27) — "sound deadening" is FOUR different jobs, and confusing them is how people waste money:
1. DAMPING — stop sheet metal ringing. Butyl/foil CLD (Kilmat, Noico, Resonix, Dynamat) straight onto bare metal. ~25–30% coverage on a large panel gets most of the benefit; full coverage is mostly wasted money and weight. Highest return per dollar on this truck.
2. DECOUPLING — thin closed-cell foam (CCF) over the CLD so the barrier floats instead of being mechanically bridged to the metal.
3. BARRIER — mass loaded vinyl (MLV), ~1 lb/ft². This is the layer that actually blocks airborne road/exhaust noise. MLV laid without CCF under it loses most of its effect — that's the mistake to avoid, and it's also why the ACC bonded "mass backing" underperforms (see the Carpet entry).
4. ABSORPTION — jute / hydrophobic melamine, kills in-cabin reflections. The carpet's heat-bonded jute already IS this layer.

TWO ROOFS, OPPOSITE TREATMENTS — she has a steel cab roof over the front seats and a REMOVABLE FIBERGLASS HARDTOP over the rear (which is why vendors sell "cab headliner" and "removable hard top headliner" as separate parts). Front/steel: classic CLD territory — steel rings, so ~25% on the spans between the ribs, then a light absorber. Rear/fiberglass: fiberglass doesn't ring like steel, so CLD's return drops sharply — absorber for rain impact matters more, and WEIGHT IS A HARD CONSTRAINT because that top gets lifted off by hand. No MLV up there.

FLOOR + TUNNEL is where the thick stack pays. The transmission tunnel is the loudest AND hottest surface on a 351W truck, so MLV there doubles as a heat barrier.

RULES:
• NEVER lay butyl over rust or bare metal — it traps moisture and rots the pan under a sealed layer. Repair and paint first (the sequence already does this).
• Don't seal over the floor drain plugs. Water that gets in has to get out — especially with a removable top.
• Wipe every surface with isopropyl and use a roller. Contamination kills butyl adhesion, and unrolled CLD is decorative.
• The stack adds ~0.4" of floor height (CLD ~2mm + CCF ~6mm + MLV ~2.4mm) — see the fitment trap in the Carpet entry before committing thickness anywhere.

SEQUENCE: rust repair → interior paint → CLD → CCF → MLV (floor/tunnel, not the top) → carpet + headliner in.

CORRECTION 2026-07-27 — an earlier pass here over-specified the prep. Butyl needs a CLEAN, SOUND surface, NOT a freshly painted one. Intact factory coating is actually the better substrate because it's already cured. So the prep is a FORK you take after looking, not a fixed ritual: just dirty → vacuum, degrease, dry, deaden, same session, no cure gate (the likely case); surface rust or flaking → treat it, but for the panel's survival, not the deadener's, because sealing rust under butyl is how you find a hole in five years; perforated → different job entirely. PAINT ONLY BUYS A CURE GATE, and in this build the gate is FREE — the panels and interior are apart for the shop anyway, so there are months, not a weekend. Painting hidden cavities because you want them clean is a perfectly good reason; it just isn't a requirement.

CAVITY WAX — after deadening, shoot Fluid Film / Woolwax into the bottoms of the doors (and any other closed cavity that's open) and confirm the drains run. Doors and rockers rot bottom-up from the INSIDE, and this teardown is the only time that access will ever exist. ~$20. Order matters: deaden first, wax after — you cannot deaden over wax.

PAINTED CARGO FLOOR CHANGES THE REAR PLAN — with the bed staying Cabernet (see 'Carpet'), there's no hidden layer to stack on top back there, so rear-floor treatment moves to the UNDERSIDE of the bed floor, applied from beneath the truck. No MLV in the cargo area at all if the floor shows.

Door specifics live with the teardown protocol in guides/bolores-door-panel-repair.md (STEP 6): don't seal the door drains, and go easy on mass in a door — OBS Ford doors are heavy and sag-prone, so CLD on the outer skin + foam on the inner, not a pile of MLV.

CARGO FLOOR — REVISED 2026-07-27 (supersedes the painted-floor note directly above, which assumed an exposed bed, AND a since-removed note that assumed original paint was being preserved). ACTUAL STATE: the bed gets a FRESH factory-colour respray and then CARPET over it. So there is no original-paint constraint back there and no reason to avoid bonding — the cargo floor is treated like any other floor: CLD bonded on top, CCF, MLV, carpet. Simpler and acoustically better than the loose-laid workaround that was briefly recorded here.

THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS THE CURE GATE — that bed paint is FRESH, so butyl doesn't go on it until it has fully cured, or the solvent still outgassing underneath lifts the deadener later. Costs nothing here: the truck is apart anyway (see the free-cure-gate note above).

✅ CARGO FLOOR RESOLVED 2026-07-27 (Paul) — NOTHING GETS BONDED BACK THERE. The cargo carpet simply RESTS on the painted bed; no adhesive, no deadener bonded to the floor. This is also how molded kits normally go in — the cargo section is held by its own molded shape plus the wheel-well covers, sill plates and belt bolts; gluing is mostly a front-footwell/tunnel thing where carpet wants to creep.

Three things fall out, all favourable: (1) it makes the WATER story better, not just simpler — the standing 'pull the rear carpet after a real soaking' practice (see 'Carpet') is only possible with loose carpet; bonded carpet can't be lifted and dried, and this truck has the leak history that makes that matter; (2) the REVEAL survives — lift it, see the fresh Cabernet, which was the point of carpeting rather than leaving it bare; (3) NO CURE GATE back there, so the bed's respray timing stops constraining anything.

THE TRADE: no CLD damping on the cargo floor. It's a big flat panel and it will drum a little. Spend nothing on it now — it's the least important surface back there, the carpet's jute gives absorption, and the transmission tunnel is what actually gets noticed. The fix stays fully available later and never touches the paint: DAMP IT FROM THE UNDERSIDE, worked from beneath the truck. Revisit only when the amp + subs go in (Phase 5) — bass on an undamped floor is the one case where it'd be audible.

If the mat ever wanders under loading: hook-and-loop tabs or snap fasteners give retention without committing to adhesive.

Researched + decided 2026-07-27. A MOLDED, VEHICLE-SPECIFIC KIT IS THE CALL — not bulk roll carpet. The realistic alternative means templating and seaming a two-door Bronco's tunnel and wheel wells by hand: days of work for a worse result, and the kit costs less than a trim shop's labor alone.

WHAT TO BUY — the vendors are reselling ONE product: Auto Custom Carpets (ACC), made in USA. Bronco Graveyard $339 (listed 87–93); Stock Interiors $362.95 (87–96, base plush cut pile). LMC sells the same class of kit and is very likely also ACC-sourced, but that's unconfirmed — their site blocks automated reads (403), so LMC's price is UNVERIFIED. So you're choosing a retailer and a spec, not a brand; Bronco Graveyard is cheapest of the three for the same kit.

WHAT THE "COMPLETE" KIT INCLUDES: passenger area + rear cargo + wheel well covers, with mildew-resistant jute heat-bonded to the back where padding was factory, and the heel pad positioned. NO padding in the rear cargo area.

DECIDED — SKIP THE MASS BACKING (+$125 Bronco Graveyard / +$145 Stock Interiors). It's a thin rubber layer bonded to the carpet, FRONT SECTION ONLY, and being glued to the carpet it can't be decoupled — a compromised version of the MLV layer the soundproofing build does properly and cheaper. Forum owners also report the mass-backed version is noticeably harder to make lie flat. (If the full CLD/CCF/MLV build ever gets abandoned, mass backing becomes the cheap shortcut — that's the only case for it.)

KNOWN FIT ISSUES (fullsizebronco.com): molding is "not very well defined like original" — it arrives oversized in places and you trim it down. The TRANSMISSION TUNNEL is the trouble spot (one owner with the bigger E4OD hump gave up and covered the tunnel separately; the AOD hump is smaller, so lower risk — but test-fit the tunnel before cutting anything). WHEEL-WELL COVERS are the fiddliest piece, a two-person job — check the overlap with the rear section before cutting. Cutting the holes (seat bolts, belt anchors, shifter, 4WD lever) is the hard part: measure from underneath, cut small, open up. Heat gun or steamer to re-mold the backing to the pan. It settles over a few days once the seats bolt down and hold it flat.

⚠️ FITMENT TRAP — the deadening stack raises the floor ~0.4", and the carpet was molded for FACTORY thickness. Put the thick stack where it pays (tunnel + flat floor), keep it thin in the footwells and away from the pedals, and keep it OUT FROM UNDER THE SEAT RISER FEET entirely — do NOT solve a raised floor with longer bolts, because seat and belt anchors are structural and thread engagement isn't the place to improvise. Test-fit the carpet over the FINISHED deadening before cutting a single hole.

COLOR GATE — match the AFTERMARKET LEATHER and the sprayed chestnut, NOT the 1989 factory chart (see 'Driver seat upholstery': the seats aren't factory). ACC charges a 30% RESTOCKING FEE on returned carpet, so there's one shot: order the free swatches now and judge them in daylight against the leather. (Forum datapoint, UNVERIFIED: '89 Eddie Bauer tan trim = "Light Chestnut," code 9T.)

SEQUENCE — Phase 4, and LAST: order swatches now, but buy only after the floor is painted and the deadening is in. Gate cleared 2026-07-27: the tailgate leak itself is fixed (see 'Bed rust'), so the remaining gate is the metal repair + paint.

⚠️ COLLISION SURFACED 2026-07-27 — THE BED IS STAYING CABERNET RED (see 'Full repaint'), and the ACC "complete kit" carpets the passenger area PLUS REAR CARGO PLUS WHEEL WELLS. You can't spray the bed body-colour to show it off and then carpet over it. DECIDE BEFORE ORDERING — it changes which kit gets bought:
• Carpeted cargo area — more original for an Eddie Bauer, quieter, warmer. Hides the red.
• Painted cargo area — sportier and more truck-like, easy to hose out, better for hauling.
• MIDDLE PATH (looks deliberate on a Bronco, and is the recommendation): carpet the WHEEL WELLS and side panels — which are the big resonant surfaces anyway — leave the FLOOR red, and throw a removable mat over it when hauling.

CONSEQUENCE — a visible painted floor has nowhere to hide the deadening stack. No CCF/MLV on top of a show surface, so rear treatment has to move to the UNDERSIDE of the bed floor, worked from beneath the truck. Different job, different product; plan it in rather than discovering it.

UNCONFIRMED, worth a phone call to Bronco Graveyard before ordering: whether a PASSENGER-AREA-ONLY kit even exists for this truck. Every vendor listing found is "complete kit" (ACC lists complete kits across 87-93 and 94-96; Stock Interiors' category page 404'd). Cargo-area pieces ARE sold separately elsewhere, so a front-only kit probably exists — but it isn't verified.

Also unverified: whether the kit includes a tailgate cover — some ACC listings explicitly exclude it.

✅ DECIDED 2026-07-27 (Paul) — BUY THE COMPLETE KIT, rear cargo carpeted. The bed is factory-COLOURED and is getting a fresh respray in that colour (see 'Full repaint' — an earlier reading here had it as preserved original paint; that was an agent misread, corrected same day). His call is to re-cover it: carpet goes back over the fresh paint, protecting it, and lifts out any time he wants to look at the bed. That also resolves the collision above and moots the open "does a passenger-area-only kit exist" question — complete is what every vendor sells anyway, so it's one less call. It restores the absorber layer for the audio build, and it's the Eddie Bauer-correct answer, which lines up with the factory-two-tone-protects-resale logic already driving the paint.

MAINTENANCE PRACTICE that comes with the decision: carpet + jute over the bed floor will hold water against the paint if water gets in, and this truck has exactly that history. Keep the bed drains clear, and treat "pull the rear carpet after a real soaking" as a standing practice — the removability is doing double duty, not just serving as a party trick.

📍 2026-07-27 (Paul): the OLD interior carpeting is ALREADY OUT — he stripped it, cargo floor is bare. So nothing is holding moisture against the floor any more, and the new kit lands on a clean slate whenever the floor work and paint are done.

restoration.item: Fall put-away — oil change + drain the carb
restoration.detail: Autumn 2026, a fall evening in the shop. Paul's call 2026-07-27, and it's the better order: fresh oil sits far better over winter than used oil, which carries a little acid and moisture the whole time it sits. So this REPLACES the spring oil change rather than adding to it. Calendar reminder set for the first Saturday of November, recurring yearly — but the date is a placeholder for "too cold to ride," not a deadline; move it to whichever evening the riding actually ends (first frost here averages Oct 17). THE JOB: warm her up, drain the oil, new filter (Suzuki 16510-37450 / HiFlo HF138), refill ~1.0 qt 10W-40 JASO MA/MA2. Then DRAIN THE FLOAT BOWL on the Mikuni BST31SS — this is the one that actually matters for her. Stale fuel varnishing in the carb is exactly what cost her the drain-and-flush in May 2025, and an empty bowl can't varnish. Tires to 22 psi front / 25 rear, chain cleaned and lubed. BOTH BIKES: fill the tank most of the way with the ethanol-free gas they already run — less air space, less condensation. Battery off the bike, on a tender or somewhere it won't freeze (that's what worked last time). Cover her.

Spring 2027. If the fall put-away went as above, this is a small morning, not a project: battery back on, fresh fuel, prime the carb, check tires and chain, ride. A full carb clean should NOT be needed — draining the bowl in the fall is what buys that. Only pull the bowl if she runs lean or won't idle, which points at a clogged pilot circuit. Float height spec, if you ever are in there: 13.0 ± 1.0 mm.

restoration.item: Electrical fault — total power loss when steering
restoration.detail:
RESOLVED 2026-07-03 — Paul got the power-loss fault worked out; the bike powers up cleanly again with a constant, steady flow. THE ACTUAL FIX (not the planned conductor splice): worked the connectors up by the steering head — reseated the individual wires/pins in their plastic connector housings, cleaned the contacts with electrical contact cleaner, then pressed the connectors firmly back together; that alone restored a constant flow. Also patched a couple of questionable wire joints and wrapped everything in electrical tape for a more durable seal. So the root cause was really dirty/loose connector contacts at the flex point, not a cleanly-broken conductor. WATCH FOR RECURRENCE: the tape seal is less permanent than adhesive-lined heat-shrink, and if the fault ever returns when turning the bars, the fallback is to cut the suspect section back to bright copper and solder-splice it with adhesive heat-shrink (the originally-planned repair).

— Original diagnosis, kept for reference —
DIAGNOSED 2026-06-13 — traced end to end with a multimeter. The fault is a broken/fatigued conductor in the steering-head harness (the bundle that flexes when you turn the bars), confirmed by wiggle-testing the wires and watching the headlight cut on and off. THE TRAIL: (1) Battery good — 12.7V at the posts, both cables tight. (2) Main fuse good — there are two 20A blade fuses in the holder above the battery; the live one reads 12.7V on BOTH ends (power passes all the way through it), the second is just Suzuki's spare clipped in an unwired holder (reads nothing — normal). So power is healthy from the battery through the fuse. (3) Followed the feed forward to the green 2-pin connector up by the bars (a red wire + an orange wire): the RED wire is the always-hot feed and reads 12.7V there — power is good right up to the steering head. (4) Wiggling the harness at the steering head makes the headlight flicker on and off = a make-and-break in a conductor right where the bundle flexes with steering. This matches the original 'died when I turned the bars' symptom, and the water that killed the speedo points to the same area. ORIGINAL SYMPTOM (first test ride, June 2026): leaned the bike, turned the bars, and ALL power died at once — headlight cut instantly, no response to ignition on/off. The speedo was already removed + taped off during that ride, so a speedo short was ruled out. The carbureted DR-Z400S has no tip-over/lean sensor, so the lean didn't cut it — the wiring moved. NEXT STEPS TO CLOSE IT: (a) Disconnect the battery negative before cutting anything. (b) Pinpoint the exact inch — steady the bundle, wiggle one wire at a time to find which single wire toggles the light, then binary-search it (pinch the midpoint, flex each half, follow the half that flickers; a gentle steady pull while flexing makes the break show up sharper). Breaks usually sit right where a wire enters the back of a connector, or at a hard bend / under an old taped section. (c) Cut out the bad section back to bright clean copper; splice with solder + adhesive-lined heat-shrink (seals against the moisture history) or an adhesive-lined heat-shrink butt connector; leave a little slack so it flexes over a length, not one point, and route clear of the steering-head turn-stops. (d) While it's open, clean the green connector pins (contact cleaner + dielectric grease) — same water exposure, cheap insurance. (e) TEST: continuity-check the repaired wire with the power off, then key on -> headlight solid, then turn the bars lock-to-lock to confirm it stays lit through the full sweep, then check horn + brake light (same feed). Once power is solid, the speedo rebuild moves back to the top. SAFETY while flexing it live: keep any bare wire from touching the frame/engine or it'll pop the main fuse and send you back to square one.

Summer 2025 — the extensive carb + cooling overhaul Paul recalled (his private EXTRACTED.md note had it only as a vague recollection); the OpenAI ChatGPT conversation mine reconstructed the blow-by-blow on 2026-07-22. THE ARC: the bike started hard and would run only on the choke — a classic LEAN condition (clogged pilot / stale gas). Paul cleaned the carburetor and spark plug and installed a NiceCNC extended air/fuel mixture screw, but the old screw had sat ~5.5 turns out and the new one was reset far leaner — it wouldn't catch and backfired. Chasing it richer to ~4 turns out over-corrected into FLOODING: raw fuel leaked from the carb, a flooded cylinder strained the starter (near-hydrolock), and the plug sprayed fuel. ⚠️ SAFETY: while cranking with the plug out to clear the flood, expelled fuel vapor IGNITED — a brief garage flash-fire near the plug (no injury; a hard lesson in not cranking raw fuel near an arcing/ungrounded plug). Separately, the RADIATOR was found visibly damaged on 2025-07-11 — new radiators installed BOTH sides by 2025-07-19, cooling system refilled and bled (an initial trapped air pocket caused smoking + a red temp light until re-bled; the radiator receipt is still unfound — see private service records for the narrowed 7/11–7/19 purchase window). Final loose end: a HIGH IDLE + overheat after the carb work, traced to the idle-speed screw turned in too far (NOT the fuel screw) — backed out to spec. OUTCOME: starts reliably, the start-squeak gone. Fuel-screw baseline for this bike at ~2,900 ft elevation ≈ 1.75–2.5 turns out. Installed + confirmed running: NiceCNC extended mixture screw, DRZ400 air filter, NGK CR8E plug, APE inline fuel filter.

RESOLVED SINCE (Paul-confirmed 2026-07-22): the vacuum petcock now works fine and the fuel-screw washer is back in — the bike is running very well. STILL OPEN: valve clearance has not been confirmed checked.

restoration.detail: Autumn 2026, same evening as Blue Thunder. Paul's call 2026-07-27, and it's the better order: fresh oil sits far better over winter than used oil, which carries a little acid and moisture the whole time it sits. So this REPLACES the spring oil change rather than adding to it. Calendar reminder set for the first Saturday of November, recurring yearly — but the date is a placeholder for "too cold to ride," not a deadline; move it to whichever evening the riding actually ends (first frost here averages Oct 17). THE JOB: oil 1.9 US qt with filter (Suzuki 16510-29F00 / HiFlo HF139) — DRY-SUMP, so drain BOTH plugs, crankcase and frame downtube. Drain the float bowl on the BSR36. Check coolant level and condition while you're down there — she's the only one of the two with a cooling system, and it was refilled and bled in 2025. If the evening has room, this is also the natural time to finally check VALVE CLEARANCE — still the one unconfirmed item left over from the 2025 overhaul. BOTH BIKES: fill the tank most of the way with the ethanol-free gas they already run — less air space, less condensation. Battery off the bike, on a tender or somewhere it won't freeze (that's what worked last time). Cover her.

Spring 2027. Battery back on, fresh fuel, prime, check coolant and chain, ride. Should be small if the bowl came out dry in the fall. Fuel-screw baseline for this bike at ~2,900 ft is 1.75–2.5 turns out, if she ever needs re-setting — the 2025 overhaul settled that the hard way.

restoration.detail: Summer 2025 (captured from the ChatGPT mine 2026-07-22; identified as this G22A from an ID-tag photo 2025-09-12 — earlier threads mis-guessed 'G14/G16'). After a family oil change filled it to the dipstick MAX, the cart smoked heavily and sputtered at full throttle — an OVERFILL forced oil through the crankcase breather into the intake/combustion. Draining the carb didn't help (ruled out flooding); the fix was draining + flushing the oil, refilling a measured ~1 qt, and cleaning pooled oil out of the air intake — ran well after (Paul-confirmed). A residual oil-fouled main jet caused a lingering throttle sputter into July. Separately (2025-05-04): left in the rain, ran ~1 mi on low gas then died and wouldn't restart even with starter fluid — no logged resolution, likely subsumed by the June oil work. The 'fill by measure, not to MAX' lesson is now in maintenance.engineOil.
